notes: \cpara{Opens with an earlier reply to people who say nothing is real. The linked post, ``Quantum Non-Realism'' (earlier in this book), makes the point in other words: ``even if nothing exists, I still want to understand the nothing as best I can.''}

\cpara{States the supposition. Its two halves come apart for the philosophers who hold the first. Moral error theorists, such as Mackie (1977), hold that nothing is morally right, but not that everything is permissible, since permissibility is itself a moral status. In the Stanford Encyclopedia's words (``Moral Anti-Realism''), the error theorist does not think torturing innocent people is wrong, ``but doesn't think that it is morally good or morally permissible either.''}
\cpara{Makes the supposition total: whatever the basis of the reader's moral philosophy, it is torn apart and nothing can replace it. The author says plainly that this is not a real claim.}

\cpara{A joke at the reader's certainty. The link goes to ``How to Convince Me That 2 + 2 = 3,'' where the author writes ``I find it quite easy to imagine a situation which would convince me that 2 + 2 = 3.'' On the author's view even 2 + 2 = 4 is not beyond disproof.}
\cpara{Asks the first questions: tipping, fidelity, and a child on the train tracks.}
\cpara{Shows that the supposition gives no guidance either way: without a ``should'', there is no more reason to economize than to indulge.}
\cpara{Heads off the stock picture of the nihilist, calling it a cached thought (``Cached Thoughts,'' earlier in this book).}
\cpara{Asks whether the reader would get up, and what they would do after eating.}
\cpara{Asks whether the reader would go on reading the blog and trying to be rational.}

\cpara{Ends with the question and no answer. The author's answers came the next day, in ``The Moral Void'' (30 June 2008), which the book leaves out. The next post in the book, ``Changing Your Metaethics,'' summarizes them: ``If your metaethic stops telling you to save lives, you can just drag the kid off the train tracks anyway.''}

\clogic{Philosophers who accept that nothing is morally right discuss a related question, what to do with moral language. The Stanford Encyclopedia (``Moral Anti-Realism'') describes two answers: fictionalists would keep using it without committing to moral facts, as one speaks within a story, and abolitionists would largely drop it.}
